claims.text: Mechanical wear locally refines the HEA surface into an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer rapidly forms a stable passive oxide film.
A regenerating protective surface simultaneously mitigates wear and corrosion.
Cyclic wear in an oxygen-containing corrosive electrolyte triggers both dynamic surface refinement and passive-film reformation.
Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures provide sufficient diffusion for the proposed response.
The required sliding conditions must repeatedly disrupt and reform the passive film.
The refined near-surface layer contains abundant grain boundaries.
Grain boundaries in the refined layer serve as sites for rapid oxide-film regeneration.
Mechanical wear disrupts the existing passive film.
Mechanical wear induces dynamic recrystallization that produces nanoscale grains.
Fine grains enhance atomic diffusion and thereby accelerate repassivation.
The reformed oxide layer limits both mechanical material removal and corrosive attack.
A dynamically refined HEA surface will have a lower total degradation rate than a coarse-grained passive-film baseline.
The refined surface will exhibit reduced wear volume relative to the coarse-grained baseline.
The refined surface will exhibit lower corrosion current density relative to the coarse-grained baseline.
The mechanism should operate only when wear is sufficient to refine the surface and oxidizing species are available to form a passive oxide.
The mechanism may fail when wear is too weak to induce nanocrystallization or when the environment cannot support oxide formation.
A controlled test should compare composition-matched specimens with pre-engineered ultra-nanocrystalline and coarse-grained surfaces under identical tribo-corrosion conditions.
Failure of the refined specimens to improve wear, corrosion, or passive-film robustness relative to the coarse baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as not undergoing wear-induced nanostructural transformation, but the proposed coarse-grained control is subjected to the same cyclic sliding conditions that are supposed to trigger that transformation. Without verifying that the control remains coarse-grained, the stated baseline may not be maintained.

The hypothesis assigns causality to dynamically wear-induced refinement, whereas the experiment substitutes a pre-engineered nanocrystalline surface. This tests the effect of the refined state but does not directly isolate whether dynamic refinement during wear is the governing cause.
